title: Is AI about to herald a golden age of custom solutions for schools and trusts?
author: Doug O’Brien and Lucy Gambier
summary: Doug O'Brien and Lucy Gambier of CELT ask whether multi-academy trusts should still start by shopping for software now that AI makes building bespoke applications feasible. They describe building an alternative provision tracker, an HR platform, a complaints system and a line management and meetings app inside their Microsoft environment, using AI chat to turn requirements into working code. The case is that a custom tool can start from the trust's own policy and process and can bring data such as attendance dashboards into the same place as meeting notes. They sketch three futures for trust software: continued specialist platforms, consolidation around the MIS, and trust-built applications. The authors are careful about costs and risks, noting licences, storage, staff time, support, security design and the danger of depending on one person who built a tool. Their view is that educational understanding of the problem is the scarce skill, and the bigger prize is better decisions rather than licence savings.
points: AI chat tools let a small team describe requirements and iterate on working applications, shortening the distance between understanding an organisational problem and building a response.
Building inside an established platform such as Microsoft's Power Platform and Dataverse provides role-based access control, though permissions still need design and testing.
The honest cost comparison must include licensing, storage, staff time, support and the risk when the builder leaves, and building shifts rather than removes supplier dependence.
Trusts may end up with three overlapping models: specialist software, an MIS-centred suite, and selected in-house applications.
The authors see the greater payoff in connected data that improves leadership decisions about provision, complaints and capacity, not in licence savings.
quotes: At CELT, we have been using AI to help generate the code for custom applications within our own Microsoft environment.

A relatively small number of people have been able to make substantial progress in a short period of time. AI chat interfaces allow us to describe requirements, develop functionality and work through changes without assembling a conventional team of specialist software developers.
There is still technical work involved. Getting something to appear on a screen is a different achievement from making it reliable enough for colleagues to depend on.
The third is a growing space for trusts to develop applications of their own, using AI alongside established platforms for hosting, data and access management.
AI can help turn those requirements into software. It cannot be relied on to decide whether the requirements make educational or organisational sense.
A working application also needs a future. Who supports it when something fails? Can someone else understand how it works? What happens when the person who built it leaves?
Nor does building on Microsoft remove reliance on a supplier. It changes that reliance.
When a trust knows exactly what it needs, how often will buying the nearest available product still be the best answer?
